```{r, include = FALSE}
library(ADMIT)
```

## Overview

This vignette walks through choosing the inclusion window for an admixture-mapping scan with ADMIT.
The workflow has three steps:

1. measure the background false-call rate ε₀ of your local-ancestry caller in your own cohort;
2. choose a reliability curve: a shipped curve, a shipped curve rescaled to your caller, or one you
   calibrate;
3. compute the detection- and estimation-optimal windows.

The examples use 52,639 UK Biobank participants with RFMix v2 calls and African as the focal
ancestry. Steps that need individual-level data are shown with their output rather than run.

## Why reliability sets a window

Admixture mapping regresses a trait on local ancestry, so each individual contributes information in
proportion to the variance of their local ancestry across the genome, 2q(1 − q). This variance
vanishes as global ancestry q approaches 0 or 1. The caller's error does not: an individual who
carries no focal ancestry still receives focal calls at a background rate ε₀. Reliability, the share
of an individual's called variance that is signal, therefore falls steeply at low q:

```{r}
q <- 10^seq(-4, -0.5, length.out = 200)
plot(q, adm_reliability(q, eps0 = 1.4e-3), type = "l", log = "x", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "global focal ancestry q", ylab = "reliability")
```

An individual raises the power of the scan only when their reliability exceeds about half the pooled
reliability of those already included. This half-reliability rule turns into a window on global
ancestry whose lower bound sits at a few multiples of ε₀.

## Step 1: measure ε₀

`adm_eps0()` takes the global ancestry proportions and the genome-wide mean focal local-ancestry
dosage of each individual. It estimates ε₀ from individuals who are near-pure in a non-focal ancestry:

```{r eval = FALSE}
eps <- adm_eps0(global_Q, local_dosage = my_dosage, focal = "AFR", pure_cut = 0.99)
eps
#> Background false-call rate for focal AFR
#>   eps0 = 0.000587   (sd across the reference group 0.000825)
#>   reference: 39,069 of 52,639 individuals, >99% in a single non-focal ancestry
```

The reference group is defined on the other ancestries. Selecting individuals whose focal estimate is
near zero would keep the ones the caller got right and underestimate ε₀. For South Asian ancestry in
UK Biobank, the focal-estimate rule keeps 1,956 individuals, whereas the non-focal rule keeps 38,899
and measures the higher rate the caller actually has.

## Step 2: choose a reliability curve

ADMIT ships reliability curves for African and South Asian focal ancestry. They were measured on
16,000 simulated genomes built from held-out founders and called by RFMix v2 against a five-ancestry
HGDP + 1000 Genomes reference:

```{r}
head(adm_curve("AFR"), 4)
```

A measured curve is the default because the one-parameter closed form in `adm_reliability()` gets
the scaling with ε₀ right but not the level. On the UK Biobank cohort:

| | closed form | measured curve |
|---|---|---|
| reliability at q̂ ≈ 0.001 | 0.59 | **0.15** |
| detection-optimal cut | 0.0021 | **0.0038** |
| efficiency at that cut | 0.97 (claimed) | **0.84** |

The closed form places the cut about twofold too tight and reports an efficiency the scan does not
reach; at its cut the measured efficiency is 0.83. `adm_threshold()` warns when it is used without a
curve.

### Transferring a curve to another caller

Reliability depends on global ancestry through q/ε₀, so a curve measured for one caller transfers to
another by rescaling with the ratio of their background rates. RFMix and FLARE, run on the same
simulated genomes, differ 2.4-fold in ε₀ (1.33 × 10⁻³ and 3.19 × 10⁻³), and their curves agree on the
rescaled axis:

| q/ε₀ | 0.4 | 1.5 | 7.5 | 38 | 150 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reliability, RFMix | 0.284 | 0.552 | 0.848 | 0.942 | 0.955 |
| reliability, FLARE | 0.255 | 0.574 | 0.848 | 0.943 | 0.952 |

The median disagreement across 0.38 < q/ε₀ < 319 is 0.005. On the 52,639-person cohort, a FLARE user
choosing the window from the rescaled RFMix curve attains an efficiency of 0.858, against 0.859 from
FLARE's own curve and 0.843 without rescaling:

```{r eval = FALSE}
cur <- adm_rescale(adm_curve("AFR"), eps0_from = 1.33e-3, eps0_to = eps)
```

### Calibrating a curve for a new caller

For a caller or reference panel unlike the shipped ones, calibrate a curve directly. ADMIT holds out
founders, simulates admixed genomes with your cohort's ancestry distribution, and scores your
caller's output against the known truth. You run the caller yourself:

```{r eval = FALSE}
split <- adm_holdout(ref_pop, frac = 0.25)            # founders the caller will not see

sim <- adm_simulate(hap, hap_pop, site, map,
                    q_dist = global_Q$AFR,            # your cohort's ancestry distribution
                    focal = "AFR", out_dir = "sim/")  # writes sim/sim_query.vcf

# run your caller on sim/sim_query.vcf against the reduced reference panel, then:
cur <- adm_score(sim, called = "sim/calls.msp.tsv", format = "msp")
```

`adm_score()` reads RFMix and Gnomix `.msp.tsv` output, FLARE ancestry VCFs, or a pre-parsed matrix.
Simulate genome-wide: the window is set where focal tracts are rarest, and an individual with
q = 0.005 carries on average 1.4 focal tracts across the genome but 0.03 on chromosome 22.

## Step 3: compute the window

```{r eval = FALSE}
th <- adm_threshold(q_hat = global_Q$AFR, curve = "AFR", eps0 = eps)
th
#> Inclusion window  [measured curve]
#>
#>   detection optimum    0.00382   efficiency 0.840   keeps 3,705
#>   estimation optimum   0.00568   efficiency 0.833   keeps 2,321
#>
#>   recommended window   0.00382 to 0.00568
plot(th)
```

The detection optimum maximizes the non-centrality of the test. The estimation optimum minimizes the
mean squared error of the effect estimate, because a looser window shrinks the standard error but
attenuates the estimate. Any cut between the two serves both purposes. Efficiency is flat near its
maximum, so a twofold change in the cut costs less than 0.02 and the window can be reported to one
significant figure.

To evaluate cuts you are considering, including a convention you want to compare against, use
`adm_efficiency()`. It returns the number of individuals retained, the efficiency, and the
attenuation factor R:

```{r eval = FALSE}
adm_efficiency(global_Q$AFR, curve = "AFR", cuts = c(0.002, 0.005, 0.02, 0.05))
```

On UK Biobank, ADMIT returns 0.0038–0.0057 for African and 0.0054–0.016 for South Asian ancestry.
The South Asian window is wider because RFMix assigns South Asian ancestry to unadmixed individuals at
a higher rate.

## Using the window in a scan

The window optimizes the contrast between the focal ancestry and the reference ancestry. In cohorts
with more than two ancestries, model the local dosages of the other non-reference ancestries in the
association test itself; narrowing the window does not remove their contribution and costs
information.
